content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Define reversible reactions and use the reversibility symbol
Explain how conditions affect the direction of reversible reactions
Distinguish between reversible and irreversible reactions
Most chemical reactions we encounter are
- they go in one direction only. However, many important reactions are
, meaning they can go both forwards and backwards. Understanding reversible reactions is crucial for industrial chemistry.
A reaction that can proceed in both the forward and reverse directions.
A + B → C + D (left to right)
C + D → A + B (right to left)
White solid disappears when heated, reappears when cooled
[DIAGRAM: Tube heated at bottom showing NH₄Cl subliming, reforming as white solid at cool top]
Heating drives off water (forward) - blue → white
Adding water reverses it (reverse) - white → blue
Used as a test for water
Used in weather indicators (colour change with humidity)
The forward and reverse reactions have
So the reverse reaction has ΔH = -176 kJ/mol
Changing conditions can favour either the forward or reverse reaction:
Cooling favours reverse → white → blue (if water present)
Reaction goes to completion in one direction
Example: Heating NH₄Cl in open tube - gases escape, no reverse
Example: Heating NH₄Cl in sealed tube
Write the equation for the reversible decomposition of ammonium chloride, using the correct symbol.
The ⇌ symbol shows the reaction is reversible.
Hydrated copper sulfate (blue) can be converted to anhydrous copper sulfate (white) by heating. Explain how you could reverse this change.
Add water to the white anhydrous copper sulfate
The forward reaction for decomposing ammonium chloride is endothermic (ΔH = +176 kJ/mol). What is the enthalpy change for the reverse reaction?
The reverse reaction has the opposite enthalpy change
The reverse reaction (formation of NH₄Cl) is exothermic
Explain why heating ammonium chloride in an open tube causes it to disappear completely, but in a closed tube the solid partially reforms on cooling.
NH₄Cl decomposes to NH₃ and HCl gases
Solid reforms on the cooler parts
Using a single arrow for reversible reactions
Forgetting that ΔH values are opposite for forward and reverse
If forward is +x kJ, reverse is -x kJ
can go both forwards and backwards
Examples: NH₄Cl ⇌ NH₃ + HCl, CuSO₄·5H₂O ⇌ CuSO₄ + 5H₂O
If forward is endothermic, reverse is exothermic
Products escape, reaction goes to completion
Conditions (temperature, concentration) affect which direction is favoured
